egmo-2015-01.title: F is an excentre of BDC
egmo-2015-01.body:
Let $\angle ABC=2\beta$.

**Where $F$ is.** $B$ lies on line $AD$ outside segment $AD$, so $B$ is outside $\omega$, and $E$, $F$ lie on the same ray from $B$. Hence $F$ is on the same side of $AB$ as $C$. As $\angle ADC=90^\circ$ and $\angle ADF=45^\circ$, ray $DF$ bisects the right angle $ADC$. So line $DF$ is the **external** bisector of $\angle BDC$ in triangle $BDC$, while line $BF$ is the internal bisector of $\angle DBC$. These two lines meet only at the excentre of triangle $BDC$ opposite $B$. So $F$ is that excentre, and therefore $CF$ is the external bisector of $\angle BCD$.

**Angles.** In triangle $BDC$: $\angle DBC=2\beta$, $\angle BDC=90^\circ$, $\angle BCD=90^\circ-2\beta$. The exterior angle at $C$ is $90^\circ+2\beta$, so
$$\angle ECF=\angle DCF=45^\circ+\beta .$$
$E$ lies between $D$ and $C$ and between $B$ and $F$, so $\angle CEF=\angle DEB=90^\circ-\beta$ (vertical angles, in the right triangle $BDE$). Therefore, in triangle $CEF$,
$$\angle CFE=180^\circ-(45^\circ+\beta)-(90^\circ-\beta)=45^\circ .$$

**Tangency.** $\angle FDE=\angle FDC=45^\circ=\angle CFE$, and $C$ and $D$ lie on opposite sides of line $EF$ (since $E$ lies between them). By the converse of the tangent–chord theorem, $CF$ is tangent to the circle through $D,E,F$, which is $\omega$. ∎

egmo-2015-02.title: One domino per block, then two staircases
egmo-2015-02.body:
Split the board into $n^2$ aligned $2\times2$ **blocks**. A $2\times2$ square is *good* if some whole row or column of it is uncovered, i.e. if its covered cells lie within one row or one column.

**1. Each block holds exactly one domino.** A good square has at most $2$ covered cells. The $n^2$ dominoes cover $2n^2$ cells, so every block has exactly $2$ covered cells, lying in one row or one column.

Suppose a horizontal domino $d$ straddles two blocks $X$ (left) and $Y$, covering $(r,2j)$ and $(r,2j+1)$ (row $r$, columns $2j$, $2j+1$). Let $r'$ be the other row of the block-row. The square on rows $r,r'$ and columns $2j,2j+1$ is good, so $(r',2j)$ and $(r',2j+1)$ are uncovered. In $X$, $(r,2j)$ is covered and $(r',2j)$ is not, so the second covered cell of $X$ is $(r,2j-1)$. It is covered by a domino $d_1\ne d$, and we check the possibilities:
- $d_1$ cannot be vertical inside $X$, as $X$ would have $3$ covered cells.
- $d_1$ cannot be vertical crossing into the next block-row. Applying the same argument to $d_1$ would force the cells of column $2j$ in those two rows to be uncovered, but $(r,2j)\in d$.

So $d_1$ is horizontal on columns $2j-2,2j-1$: another straddling domino, further left. Repeating this runs off the board, a contradiction. Vertical dominoes are handled the same way. So no domino straddles, and each block contains exactly one domino. Call the block **top**, **bottom**, **left** or **right** according to its position.

**2. Two adjacent blocks.** Let $S_1=\{\text{right},\text{bottom}\}$ and $S_2=\{\text{left},\text{bottom}\}$.
- *$X$ directly left of $Y$.* The middle square is $X$'s right column plus $Y$'s left column. Checking the $16$ cases, it is good exactly for the pairs (left, any), (top, top), (top, right), (bottom, bottom), (bottom, right), (right, right). These are exactly the pairs with ($X\in S_1\Rightarrow Y\in S_1$) and ($Y\in S_2\Rightarrow X\in S_2$).
- *$X$ directly above $Y$.* The good pairs are (top, any), (left, left), (left, bottom), (right, right), (right, bottom), (bottom, bottom). These are exactly the pairs with ($X\in S_1\Rightarrow Y\in S_1$) and ($X\in S_2\Rightarrow Y\in S_2$).

So the set $\mathcal S_1$ of blocks of type in $S_1$ is closed under moving **right and down**, and the set $\mathcal S_2$ of blocks of type in $S_2$ is closed under moving **left and down**. The type of a block is determined by its membership in $\mathcal S_1$ and $\mathcal S_2$: right $=(1,0)$, bottom $=(1,1)$, left $=(0,1)$, top $=(0,0)$.

**3. The remaining squares are automatically good.** A square meeting four blocks $X$ (top-left), $Y$, $Z$, $W$ (bottom-right) consists of:
- $a$, the bottom-right cell of $X$, covered iff $X\in\mathcal S_1$;
- $b$, the bottom-left cell of $Y$, covered iff $Y\in\mathcal S_2$;
- $c$, the top-right cell of $Z$, covered iff $Z\notin\mathcal S_2$;
- $d$, the top-left cell of $W$, covered iff $W\notin\mathcal S_1$.

If $X\in\mathcal S_1$ then $W\in\mathcal S_1$ by closure, so $a$ and $d$ are not both covered. Likewise, if $Y\in\mathcal S_2$ then $Z\in\mathcal S_2$, so $b$ and $c$ are not both covered. A set of covered cells containing neither diagonal pair lies in one row or column, so the square is good. Squares inside one block are good as well. So a placement is valid **iff** $\mathcal S_1$ is right-down closed and $\mathcal S_2$ is left-down closed, with any such pair allowed.

**4. Counting.** A right-down closed set is determined by its row lengths $0\le k_1\le k_2\le\dots\le k_n\le n$ (each row contains a suffix, and the suffixes lengthen going down). There are $\binom{2n}{n}$ such sequences (monotone lattice paths). The same holds for left-down closed sets.

**Answer: $\binom{2n}{n}^2$.**

egmo-2015-03.title: Pigeonhole on the gcd values
egmo-2015-03.body:
Assume $a_1=\min a_i$.

**Easy case: $a_1\ge n^m-1$.** Then every $a_i\in\{n^m-1,n^m\}$.
- If all $a_i$ are equal, take $b_1=1$, $b_2=2$ (others arbitrary). Then the gcd divides $\gcd(a_1+1,a_1+2)=1$.
- Otherwise $a_1=n^m-1$ and some $a_j=n^m$. Take $b_1=b_j=1$; the gcd divides $\gcd(n^m,n^m+1)=1$.

Either way the gcd is $1<n$.

**Main case: $a_1\le n^m-2$.** Suppose, for contradiction, that every choice of $(b_1,\dots,b_m)\in\{1,\dots,n\}^m$ gives a gcd $\ge n$. This gcd is at most $a_1+b_1\le n^m+n-2$. So it takes one of at most $(n^m+n-2)-n+1=n^m-1$ values, while there are $n^m$ choices. By pigeonhole, two different tuples $(b_i)\ne(b_i')$ give the same gcd $d\ge n$.

Pick $i$ with $b_i\ne b_i'$. Then $d\mid a_i+b_i$ and $d\mid a_i+b_i'$, so $d\mid b_i-b_i'$. But $0<|b_i-b_i'|\le n-1<d$. Contradiction.

Hence some choice gives $\gcd<n$. ∎

egmo-2015-04.title: Consecutive differences
egmo-2015-04.body:
Suppose such a sequence exists. For $n\ge2$ let $b_n=a_{n+1}-a_n$. The recurrence (with index $n-1$) says $b_n=\sqrt{a_n+a_{n-1}}$, so each $b_n$ ($n\ge2$) is a positive integer. For $n\ge2$,
$$b_{n+1}^2-b_n^2=(a_{n+1}+a_n)-(a_n+a_{n-1})=a_{n+1}-a_{n-1}=b_n+b_{n-1} .$$

For $n\ge3$ the right side is positive, so $b_{n+1}>b_n$. Thus $b_3<b_4<b_5<\cdots$, and in particular $b_{n+1}-b_n\ge1$ for $n\ge 3$.

Take $n=4$:
$$b_4+b_3=(b_5-b_4)(b_5+b_4)\ge b_5+b_4,$$
so $b_3\ge b_5$, contradicting $b_3<b_4<b_5$.

So no such sequence exists. (The argument uses only $a_1,\dots,a_6$.) **Answer: No.**

egmo-2015-05.title: Three partitions
egmo-2015-05.body:
We give three partitions; for each $n$ one of them works.

**Partition 1: $\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\dots,\{2m-1,2m\}$.** Boris's sum is $\sum(2i-1)+k=m^2+k$, where $k\in\{0,\dots,m\}$ is the number of even numbers chosen. So the possible sums are exactly $m^2,\dots,m^2+m$. This works for every $n\notin[m^2,m^2+m]$.

**Partition 2: $\{1,2m\},\{2,3\},\{4,5\},\dots,\{2m-2,2m-1\}$.** The $m-1$ pairs $\{2i,2i+1\}$ contribute between $\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}2i=m^2-m$ and $m^2-1$. So the total lies in $[m^2-m+1,\,m^2]$ if Boris picks $1$, and in $[m^2+m,\,m^2+2m-1]$ if he picks $2m$. Every $n$ with $m^2<n<m^2+m$ is impossible.

**Partition 3: $\{1,2m-1\},\{2,2m\},\{3,4\},\{5,6\},\dots,\{2m-3,2m-2\}$.** For $m=2$ there are no pairs after the first two. The $m-2$ pairs $\{2i+1,2i+2\}$ ($1\le i\le m-2$) contribute between $m^2-2m$ and $m^2-m-2$. The first two pairs contribute $3$, $2m+1$ or $4m-1$. So the total lies in
$$[m^2-2m+3,\,m^2-m+1]\ \cup\ [m^2+1,\,m^2+m-1]\ \cup\ [m^2+2m-1,\,m^2+3m-3].$$
Since $m>1$, this misses both $m^2$ and $m^2+m$: we have $m^2-m+1<m^2$, $m^2+m-1<m^2+m<m^2+2m-1$, and $m^2+1>m^2$.

Every $n$ falls into one of the three cases, so Anastasia can always block $n$. ∎

egmo-2015-06.title: Complex numbers
egmo-2015-06.body:
Reflect everything in $BC$. Let $H'$ and $G'$ be the reflections of $H$ and $G$. Then $HG=GP'\iff H'G'=G'P$.

**Coordinates.** Take the circumcircle as the unit circle, with $BC$ horizontal and symmetric about the imaginary axis: $c=-\bar b$. Put $d=b-\bar b=2i\operatorname{Im}b$, so $\bar d=-d$, and $|\operatorname{Im} b|$ is the distance from $O$ to $BC$, which is $\cos A$ (acute triangle, $R=1$). Reflection in the line $BC$ is $z\mapsto\bar z+d$. Then
- $h=a+b+c=a+d$, so $h'=\bar h+d=\bar a=1/a$;
- $g=\frac{a+d}{3}$, $\bar g=\frac{1/a-d}{3}$, so $g'=\bar g+d=\frac{1/a+2d}{3}$ and $\bar{g'}=\frac{a-2d}{3}$.

**The point $P$.** For points on the unit circle, the chord through $a$ and $p$ consists of the $z$ with $z+ap\bar z=a+p$. Putting $z=g$:
$$p=\frac{g-a}{1-a\bar g}=\frac{d-2a}{2+ad},\qquad \bar p=\frac1p=\frac{2+ad}{d-2a}.$$
The denominators are nonzero since $g\ne a$.

**The condition.** For $u,v$ on the unit circle, $|z-u|^2-|z-v|^2=-2\operatorname{Re}\big(z(\bar u-\bar v)\big)$. So $H'G'=G'P$ iff $g'(a-\bar p)+\bar{g'}(\bar a-p)=0$. Now
$$a-\bar p=\frac{-2(a^2+1)}{d-2a},\qquad \bar a-p=\frac{2(a^2+1)}{a(2+ad)} .$$
If $a^2=-1$, then $A$ lies on the imaginary axis, the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, and $AB=AC$, which is excluded. So we may cancel $\frac23(a^2+1)$. The condition becomes
$$-\frac{1+2ad}{a(d-2a)}+\frac{a-2d}{a(2+ad)}=0\iff (a-2d)(d-2a)=(1+2ad)(2+ad).$$
Expanding, $5ad-2a^2-2d^2=2+5ad+2a^2d^2$, i.e.
$$(a^2+1)(d^2+1)=0\iff d^2=-1\iff 4(\operatorname{Im}b)^2=1\iff\cos A=\tfrac12\iff\angle CAB=60^\circ .$$
∎
